summary: Defines a MIME content type that can tunnel an ESMTP transaction through any MIME-capable transport. This lets mail commands and messages be carried as a batch inside another message. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is like putting a whole stack of mail-handling instructions in a single parcel, so the parcel can be mailed through any route that carries parcels.

subtitle: Encapsulate SMTP transactions as MIME objects for transport through non-SMTP networks.

tldr.problem: Some systems need to send SMTP mail transactions but cannot use a live SMTP server connection, or need to secure the mail envelope, or must use SMTP extensions over an extended-free transport.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2442 defines the application/batch-SMTP MIME content type, which captures an SMTP client's commands and data as a text object that can be carried by any MIME-aware transport (HTTP, regular SMTP, etc.) and then processed by a batch SMTP processor on the receiving end.
tldr.outcome: This allows offline mail handling, multi-message batching, end-to-end security for envelope information, and SMTP extension usage over limited transports. It is informational and not widely deployed.

today: RFC 2442 defines batch SMTP as an informational standard. While the technique was used historically on BITNET and some other networks, batch SMTP has not seen wide deployment in modern Internet infrastructure. Modern systems typically use other mechanisms for securing or extending SMTP (such as TLS encryption and direct SMTP over MIME transports).

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2442 defines a MIME content type called application/batch-SMTP that allows an SMTP transaction to be recorded as a text object and transported through any system that can carry MIME objects.

Normally, SMTP is an online protocol: a client connects to a server, sends commands (HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA), and waits for responses. With batch SMTP, a specialized SMTP client runs offline without a server present, issues the same commands and data, and collects the output into a MIME object. A batch SMTP processor at the destination unpacks this object and processes each command.

The RFC is informational and provides a standard definition for a technique that had been used informally on BITNET and other networks to overcome limitations.
sections.eli5: A batch SMTP object is like a recorded script of everything a mail client would say. You can mail this script through any system that understands mail packages, and when it arrives, the processor reads the script and does all those things.

sections.title: Generation and Contents
sections.content:
A batch SMTP object is created by a specialized SMTP client that operates in generator mode. The generator assumes all commands succeed (no responses are expected) and simply outputs the sequence of SMTP commands it would send to a server.

The content follows SMTP protocol rules exactly: commands like EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, and DATA, followed by the message body, followed by RSET to start another message. Lines MUST use CRLF line terminators. The entire output becomes the body of the application/batch-SMTP MIME object.

The generator MAY use ESMTP (Extended SMTP) commands and extensions such as 8bitMIME, SIZE, and NOTARY. If extensions are used, a required-extensions content type parameter lists them (defaulting to 8bitMIME,SIZE,NOTARY if omitted).
sections.eli5: The generator is a special mail client that pretends to send mail but records everything it would say instead. It writes down MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, and all the mail commands as if the server was responding OK to everything.

sections.title: Transport and Use Cases
sections.content:
Once created, a batch SMTP object can be transported by any system capable of preserving MIME content and labelling, such as HTTP or regular SMTP.

The RFC identifies several use cases: extending end-to-end security to message envelope information (not just the message body), enabling SMTP extensions like NOTARY over unextended SMTP infrastructure, and enabling multiple separate messages to be transferred in a single transactional unit.

A historical example is BITNET, which used batch SMTP to overcome the limitation of 8-character limits on user and host names. This definition also incorporates SMTP extensions, improving on that earlier approach.
sections.eli5: The batch can travel through email, web servers, or any mail system that handles MIME packages. This lets you send secure mail, handle multiple messages at once, or use fancy SMTP features through simple systems.

sections.title: Processing and Responsibilities
sections.content:
A batch SMTP processor (on the receiving end) must accept the application/batch-SMTP object and convert it back into SMTP operations. The processor assumes the responsibilities of both an SMTP server (accepting commands) and a client (handling errors that arise).

The processor MUST check that the content is labelled application/batch-SMTP and that it supports any extensions declared in the required-extensions parameter. It MUST accept any valid EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, and DATA commands, and the RSET command for multiple messages. It MUST handle 8bit MIME and accept additional parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO.

The processor SHOULD attempt to process each message only once and SHOULD track progress so that if processing is interrupted, a restart continues from the last complete message (not the beginning). If an error occurs (bad syntax, unsupported extensions, storage failure), the processor SHOULD forward the object to the postmaster for manual handling.
sections.eli5: The processor reads the recorded script of mail commands and does exactly what it says. If something goes wrong, it tries not to do the same thing twice. If it cannot understand something, it asks a human for help.

sections.title: Security and Restrictions
sections.content:
Application/batch-SMTP is a tunneling mechanism, and tunneling can enable abuse. For example, a batch SMTP tunnel could bypass relay restrictions designed to block spam.

The RFC notes that batch SMTP processors SHOULD implement access restrictions to limit processor use to authorized generators only. This is especially important if batch SMTP is used to secure message envelope information, where authentication and encryption can ensure only trusted sources submit batch objects.

The RFC also discusses the inherent issue of message duplication in SMTP synchronization. If a processor crashes partway through a batch containing multiple messages, it may reprocess an earlier message when the batch is restarted. However, this is not a new problem introduced by batch SMTP; it is inherent to SMTP protocol design. Batch SMTP implementers are simply urged not to make the problem worse.
sections.eli5: Because you can hide things inside a batch, bad people might use it to send spam or break security. The processor should only trust the people who send it batches. And if something goes wrong and the processor restarts, it might send the same message twice. This is a known problem, not unique to batch SMTP.
